title: Probability of Two Events: Sample Spaces, Tree Diagrams, Venn Diagrams and Two-Way Tables
seo_title: Year 8 Probability Worksheets: Two-Way Tables, Venn Diagrams, Tree Diagrams and Complementary Events (Free, Answer Key)
standard_text: determine all possible combinations for 2 events, using two-way tables, tree diagrams and Venn diagrams, and use these to determine probabilities of specific outcomes in practical situations
meta_desc: Free Year 8 maths worksheets on probability for the Australian Curriculum (AC9M8P02, AC9M8P01): sample spaces for two dice, complementary events, tree diagrams, Venn diagrams and two-way tables. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: List every equally likely outcome in a sample space, then count the ones that work.
key_sub: Count the overlap of a Venn diagram once. Add probabilities only for mutually exclusive events.
body_html:
How it works

When two things happen, list all the equally likely outcomes in a sample space (a grid or a list). P(event) = number of outcomes that work ÷ total number of outcomes.

In a Venn diagram, the overlap is in both groups — count it once. Two events are mutually exclusive if they cannot happen together; then P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).

Example

Two dice are rolled. Find P(total of 9).

(3,6), (4,5), (5,4), (6,3): 4 ways.

4 out of 36.

Answer: 19

Example

P(red) = 0.2, P(blue) = 0.5 on a spinner. Find P(red or blue).

Mutually exclusive, so add.

Answer: 0.7

Common mistakes

  • Counting 4 + 5 and 5 + 4 as one outcome — they are different.
  • Using 11 possible totals as the denominator for two dice instead of 36 outcomes.
  • Counting the overlap in a Venn diagram twice.
  • Adding probabilities of events that can happen at the same time.

faq.q: What is a sample space diagram?
faq.a: A table or list of every possible outcome. For two dice it is a 6 × 6 grid with 36 outcomes.

faq.q: How do I find probabilities from a Venn diagram?
faq.a: Add the numbers in the regions you need and divide by the total of all the numbers, including the ones outside the circles.
The events cannot happen at the same time, such as rolling a 2 and rolling a 5 with one die.
Two events where exactly one must happen, such as rain and no rain. Their probabilities add to 1, so P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
Multiply the number of choices for each part. 3 mains and 4 drinks give 3 × 4 = 12 meals.

items.q: Two fair dice are rolled and the scores are added. What is the probability of a sum less than 10?
items.e: Draw a 6 × 6 sample space: 36 equally likely outcomes. 30 of them give a sum less than 10, so P = 3036 = 56.

items.q: Two fair dice are rolled and the scores are multiplied. What is the probability of a product less than 3?
items.e: Draw a 6 × 6 sample space: 36 equally likely outcomes. 3 of them give a product less than 3, so P = 336 = 112.

items.q: A coin is flipped and a fair spinner with 4 equal sections (red, blue, green, yellow) is spun. How many outcomes are possible?
items.e: 2 outcomes for the coin × 4 for the spinner = 8.

items.q: A coin is flipped and a fair spinner with 5 equal sections (red, blue, green, yellow, white) is spun. How many outcomes are possible?
items.e: 2 outcomes for the coin × 5 for the spinner = 10.

items.q: A coin is flipped and a fair spinner with 3 equal sections (red, blue, green) is spun. How many outcomes are possible?

items.q: A coin is flipped and a fair spinner with 4 equal sections (red, blue, green, yellow) is spun. What is the probability of heads and yellow?
items.e: There are 2 × 4 = 8 equally likely outcomes, and only one is (heads, yellow): 18.

items.q: A coin is flipped and a fair spinner with 3 equal sections (red, blue, green) is spun. What is the probability of tails and red?

items.q: A class of 50 students has 15 who play a musical instrument. A student is chosen at random. What is the probability that the student does NOT play an instrument?
items.e: 50 − 15 = 35 students do not play, so the probability is 710.

items.q: The probability that a seed germinates is 0.49. What is the probability that it does not germinate?
items.e: Complementary events add to 1: 1 − 0.49 = 0.51.

items.q: The probability of picking a green marble from a bag is 19. What is the probability of NOT picking a green marble?

items.e: HH, HT, TH and TT: 4 outcomes.

items.q: The tree diagram shows two flips of a fair coin. What is P(two heads)?
items.e: 1 of the 4 outcomes: ½ × ½ = ¼.

items.q: The tree diagram shows two flips of a fair coin. What is P(one head and one tail)?
items.e: HT and TH: 2 of the 4 outcomes = ½.

items.q: The tree diagram shows two flips of a fair coin. What is P(at least one tail)?
items.e: Every outcome except HH: 1 − ¼ = ¾.

items.q: A coin is flipped and a fair die is rolled. How many outcomes are there?
items.e: 2 × 6 = 12 outcomes.

items.q: A family has two children. Assuming boys and girls are equally likely, what is the probability that both are girls?
items.e: GG is 1 of 4 outcomes (BB, BG, GB, GG): ¼.

items.q: A spinner can land on red, blue or green. P(red) = 0.3 and P(blue) = 0.45. What is P(red or blue)?
items.e: Red and blue cannot happen together, so add: 0.3 + 0.45 = 0.75.

items.q: A spinner can land on red, blue or green. P(red) = 0.3 and P(blue) = 0.45. What is P(green)?
A bag has 3 red, 5 blue and 2 green counters. What is P(red or green)?
items.e: 3 + 2 = 5 out of 10 = 12.

items.q: Which pair of events are mutually exclusive when one die is rolled?
c: Getting a 2 and getting an even number
Getting a 3 and getting a prime
Getting a 6 and getting a number more than 4
Getting a 2 and getting an odd number
items.e: A 2 is never odd, so getting a 2 and getting an odd number cannot happen together.

items.q: When one card is picked from a normal pack, why can you NOT add P(heart) and P(king) to find P(heart or king)?
c: The king of hearts would be counted twice
items.e: The events overlap: the king of hearts is in both, so adding counts it twice. (The answer is 16/52.)

items.q: Two fair coins are flipped. What is the probability of at least one head?
items.e: HH, HT, TH, TT: 3 of the 4 have a head: 34.

items.q: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that both show a 6?
items.e: Only (6, 6) out of 36 outcomes: 136.

items.q: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability of a double (both the same)?
items.e: (1,1), (2,2), … (6,6): 6 out of 36 = 16.

items.q: A fair die is rolled and a coin is flipped 60 times. How many times would you expect a 6 and a head?
In a class, 18 students have a sister, 12 have a brother, 5 have both and 3 have neither. How many students are in the class?
items.e: Sister only 13, both 5, brother only 7, neither 3: 13 + 5 + 7 + 3 = 28.

items.q: The probability that Leo is late is 0.2. The probability that he is on time is 0.7. What is the probability that he is early?
items.e: The three outcomes add up to 1: 1 − 0.2 − 0.7 = 0.1.

A spinner numbered 1 to 4 is spun twice and the scores are added. What is the most likely total?
items.e: Totals 2–8. 5 can be made 4 ways (1+4, 2+3, 3+2, 4+1), more than any other: 5.

items.q: A spinner numbered 1 to 4 is spun twice and the scores are added. What is P(total = 5)?
items.e: 4 of the 16 outcomes give 5: 14.
